lede: Wall Street's AI rout deepened overnight, pushing the S&P 500 and Dow into a correction and wiping out the Nasdaq's 2026 gains as Nvidia sank about 14% on reports of an SEC accounting probe.
The ASX 200 fell for a seventh straight day to 8,592.6, a 5.4% weekly drop that erased the market's gains for the year.
Xi Jinping hailed a comprehensive turnaround in ties with Australia after meeting Albanese in Shenzhen, while COP31 ran into overtime with fossil fuels cut from the draft deal.

stories.h: COP31 runs into overtime with fossil fuels cut from the draft
stories.b: The Antalya climate summit blew past its Friday deadline after the latest draft dropped any reference to phasing down fossil fuels and a US$120 billion target for helping poor countries adapt. A bloc of European, African, Latin American and Pacific nations is demanding stronger wording, while Saudi Arabia and other oil producers resist it. Chris Bowen, who is running the negotiations for Australia, said he would talk with countries through the night, and a fresh draft is not expected until Saturday.
stories.w: Australia is running the COP31 negotiations, so a weak or failed deal reflects directly on Bowen and Canberra's climate diplomacy.

stories.h: Russia launches its biggest attack of the year on Ukraine
stories.b: Russia hit Ukraine with a huge overnight missile and drone barrage, including 27 ballistic missiles, which Zelensky called the largest attack this year. It came hours after Donald Trump reportedly said a tired Putin was ready for a deal. Zelensky rejected Trump's description of Putin as a friend, calling him a killer.
stories.w: The strikes undercut the upbeat mood Trump tried to project after his meeting with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen.

stories.h: APEC wraps up with a declaration but no deal on who runs AI
stories.b: All 21 APEC economies signed off on the Shenzhen declaration, covering supply chains, digital trade and AI. But the US and China remain split over who should set global AI rules, and the Trump and Xi talks produced no tariff changes. Xi also pledged US$20 million for APEC cooperation and a new research centre in Shenzhen.
stories.w: APEC takes in most of Australia's biggest trading partners, so its push for open trade matters for exporters facing US tariffs.

stories.h: US missile reportedly strikes near Iran's Qeshm Island again
stories.b: Iran's semi official Tasnim agency said a US missile hit the outskirts of Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz, on Friday evening, with no casualties reported. Washington had not commented. It follows US strikes on a Revolutionary Guard missile site on the island earlier in the week, which officials described as defensive.
stories.w: Each flare up around Hormuz keeps a risk premium in oil prices, which feeds into Australian petrol prices.

quick.x: Turkey says it has signed deals and plans worth more than US$26 billion since COP31 began.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says the Strait of Hormuz stays shut until seven conditions are met and verified.

stories.h: SEC reportedly probing Nvidia's accounting as shares sink 14%
stories.b: Reuters reported that enforcement staff at the US Securities and Exchange Commission are looking at possible accounting issues at Nvidia, citing two people briefed on the matter. It is not clear when the inquiry began or which practices are involved, and the SEC declined to comment. Nvidia shares fell about 13% to 14%, their worst day in almost two years, and lost roughly 23% over the week.
stories.w: Nvidia is the bellwether for the whole AI trade, so any doubt about its numbers ripples through global markets, including Australian super funds that hold it.

stories.h: Anthropic slides back toward its float price on day two
stories.b: A day after jumping 17% in its record Nasdaq debut, Anthropic fell sharply on Friday, at one point trading just 5 cents above its US$83 float price. The stock pared some losses but still closed lower as the wider AI selloff hit. Analysts noted that big tech floats often stumble on day two, with focus now on its first results as a listed company.
stories.w: It is a reminder that hype at listing does not protect a stock from the broader mood, and Australian investors could not buy in at the float price anyway.

stories.h: Apple is building its own AI agent that can run your Mac
stories.b: Apple job listings, first reported by Bloomberg, describe an autonomous assistant that can control apps, browse the web and write code for users. New chief executive John Ternus is reportedly pushing for a bolder AI approach, with a launch possible by late 2027. Apple is also making it harder for rival bots to take broad control of its computers.
stories.w: Agents that act on your behalf are the next battleground in AI, and Apple's control of its devices gives it a big advantage over outside players.

stories.h: Microsoft reportedly plans for a future without OpenAI
stories.b: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman has told staff to prepare for a scenario where OpenAI cuts off access to its technology, according to The Information. Microsoft's licence runs to 2032 and there is no sign OpenAI plans to pull it. Microsoft has been building its own models, launching new coding and security models at its Ignite conference this week.
stories.w: The world's most important AI partnership is loosening, which could reshape which models power the Office tools used across Australian workplaces.

quick.x: Nvidia's shares hit a 52 week low as the SEC report added to existing legal headaches, including an export control investigation.

stories.h: Xi hails a comprehensive turnaround after meeting Albanese
stories.b: In their fifth formal meeting, held in Shenzhen, Xi praised Albanese for rebuilding the relationship and pointed to agriculture and AI as areas for more cooperation. The two agreed to make 2027 the Australia China Year of Tourism. Albanese said Australia should engage constructively and manage differences without being defined by them, before heading to Beijing for talks with Premier Li Qiang and a CEO roundtable.
stories.w: There was no immediate win on beef tariffs, so exporters will be watching the Beijing leg for anything concrete.

stories.h: Albanese tells Putin to his face to end the war
stories.b: In his APEC plenary speech, with Putin, Xi and Trump in the room, Albanese addressed the Russian leader by name and told him to end the war now. He linked the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East to trade disruption and cost of living pressures. The remarks followed criticism from Ukrainian Australians over his group photo with Putin a day earlier.
stories.w: It was a rare direct rebuke in a room built for handshakes, and it lets Albanese push back on claims he was too cosy with Putin.

stories.h: Senate committee backs the digital duty of care bill, with changes
stories.b: A Senate committee recommended passing the bill, which would make platforms take reasonable steps to prevent online harm, but said low risk sites like small businesses and religious education websites should be exempted. It also urged a right for individuals to sue over breaches. The Coalition dissented, so Labor needs the Greens to pass it in the final sitting week starting Monday.
stories.w: It would be one of the biggest changes to online rules since the under 16 social media ban, and would start a year after becoming law.

stories.h: One week out, Victoria's election looks like Wilson's to lose
stories.b: Premier Ben Carroll says the 28 November election is winnable, but polling suggests Opposition Leader Jess Wilson is in front. Wilson's net favourability sits at plus 17 against Carroll's minus 19. Carroll is touring the state by bus and has pledged to double community dental clinics at a cost of $230 million.
stories.w: A Labor loss in Victoria would add to pressure on the Albanese government, which is already sliding in federal polls.

quick.x: A YouGov poll had Labor's primary vote at 24% and Angus Taylor narrowly ahead as preferred PM, though Labor still led 51 to 49 on two party preferred.
The gas reservation bill, which needs the Coalition or the Greens to pass, still did not have the numbers as of Thursday.

stories.h: ASX falls for a seventh day, wiping out the year's gains
stories.b: The ASX 200 dropped 1.58% to 8,592.6 on Friday, its seventh straight loss, and fell 5.39% for the week, shedding almost 490 points. Tech was hit hardest on the day, down 4.7%, while materials lost about 12% over the week. Losers outnumbered winners by more than three to one.
stories.w: A rout this broad hits super balances, and comes as the jobs data has already raised recession fears.

stories.h: Wall Street's correction sets up another rough Monday
stories.b: The S&P 500 and Dow both closed more than 10% below their record highs, the definition of a correction, and the Nasdaq turned negative for 2026. The S&P 500 lost about 8.6% for the week and the Nasdaq about 10%, the worst weeks since the tariff turmoil of April 2025. Rate hike fears from the Fed have added to the AI selloff.
stories.w: Overnight US falls usually flow straight through to the ASX, so local investors should brace for more selling when trade resumes.

stories.h: Gold has its worst week in eight months, hammering local miners
stories.b: Gold fell about 9% this week to around US$3,520 an ounce, its weakest since September 2025 and more than 35% below January's record. Fed minutes showing most officials expect more rate hikes, a strong US dollar, and investors selling gold to cover tech losses all weighed. ASX gold stocks fell about 15% over the week.
stories.w: Australia is one of the world's biggest gold producers, so the slide hits miners, royalties and the share market.

stories.h: Megaport crashes 13% as shareholders hand it a first strike
stories.b: Network company Megaport slid 12.9% to $14.94 on Friday, leaving it down 17% for the week and reversing Thursday's Anthropic inspired bounce. Its AGM also delivered a first strike against the pay report. Xero and WiseTech fell too as local tech tracked Wall Street lower.
stories.w: Megaport had been sold as an AI infrastructure winner, so its fall shows how quickly that story has turned.

quick.x: The Aussie dollar sat around 66.6 US cents on Friday, near its lowest level of the year.
Accent Group's pay report drew a second strike at its AGM as the board keeps resisting Frasers' 65 cent takeover bid.
The ACCC cleared a Dexus managed trust to buy Anglicare Sydney's half share of LDK Seniors' Living.

explainer.body: Shareholders in ASX listed companies get a vote each year on the remuneration report, which sets out how executives are paid. The vote is advisory, but if 25% or more vote against it, the company gets a strike. Two strikes in a row trigger a spill vote, where shareholders decide whether the whole board must face a fresh vote within 90 days. That is why Megaport's first strike and Accent Group's second strike this week matter: they are a formal warning that investors are unhappy.

ahead.e: COP31 negotiators in Antalya work to finalise a deal in overtime.
Both houses of federal parliament sit for the last week of the year; votes expected on the digital duty of care and gas reservation bills.
October monthly CPI inflation figures released.
UK and France led working group on security guarantees for Ukraine begins.
Review window for the ACCC's Ingenia and Peet ruling closes.
